::: {.callout-tip}
#### Learning objectives
- Explain how supervised classifiers predict localisation by comparing unknown
  proteins' correlation profiles with marker profiles, and why proteins can
  only be assigned to compartments present in the training data.
- Optimise SVM parameters (`sigma`, `cost`) by cross-validation
  (`svmOptimisation`), using class weights to handle unequal class sizes, and
  assess performance using F1 scores (`getF1Scores`, `levelPlot`,
  `getParams`).
- Classify proteins with an SVM (`svmClassification`) and set
  organelle-specific score thresholds (`orgQuants`, `getPredictions`).
- Train and apply the Bayesian TAGM-MAP model (`tagmMapTrain`,
  `tagmMapPredict`), check its convergence, and threshold predictions on the
  combined localisation and outlier probabilities.
- Visualise classification results as spatial maps (`plot2D`), and compare the
  predictions of different classifiers using spatial maps, score distributions
  and cross-tabulation.
- Explain why TAGM-MAP probabilities can be overconfident, and describe
  strategies for choosing confident predictions.
:::




## Introduction

In the previous lesson we curated a set of markers that are reliable and
representative of the structure of our U-2 OS data, and stored them in the
`markers` column of our `msn` object. We can now use these markers to predict
the localisation of the remaining proteins using supervised machine learning.
Whilst unsupervised methods such as hierarchical clustering and HDBSCAN are
able to discover tight clusters of proteins with similar behaviours, these
algorithms tend to struggle when it comes to identifying compartment borders.
There are a number of supervised and semi-supervised machine learning
algorithms available within the `pRoloc` infrastructure and these differ with
respect to their data output, interpretability, and computational demand.
Ultimately, the choice of algorithm is up to the user and we would recommend
trying multiple models to determine which works best on a given set of data and
biological question of interest.

The `pRoloc` package provides a wide range of machine learning methods for
predicting protein localisation, described in its dedicated vignette
["Machine learning techniques available in pRoloc"](https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/html/pRoloc.html).
We have also published two workflows showing how to apply these methods to
correlation profiling data: one using classical machine learning
[@Breckels2018] and one using Bayesian machine learning [@Crook2019]. In this
course we focus on two complementary approaches. We start with a Support Vector
Machine (SVM), a widely used classical classifier, and then move on to a
Bayesian approach based on t-augmented Gaussian mixture (TAGM) models. Rather
than giving only a single best guess, TAGM also estimates how confident we can
be in each prediction and allows for proteins that do not fit any of the known
compartments. We focus on how to apply these methods and interpret their
results rather than on the details of the algorithms. Participants who want to
learn more about TAGM are referred to @Crook2018 and @Crook2019.

Remember that a supervised classifier can only assign proteins to the
compartments represented in the training data. Any compartment we removed from
the marker list in the previous lesson, such as the actin cytoskeleton, cannot
be predicted.


## Classification using a Support Vector Machine

Support Vector Machines (SVMs) have been widely used for protein subcellular
localisation prediction [@Itzhak2016; @Orre2019; @Christoforou2016;
@Geladaki2019; @Mulvey2017; @Schessner2023]. To understand how an SVM works,
imagine each protein as a point in space, with one axis per fraction (here,
27 axes). Marker proteins from different compartments sit in
different regions of this space. An SVM learns **boundaries** (hyperplanes)
that separate these regions, placing each boundary as far as possible from the
markers on either side. Unknown proteins are then classified according to
which side of the boundaries they fall on. For more details about SVM
algorithms readers are directed to @Noble2006.

Real compartments rarely have straight-line boundaries, so the SVM uses a
**kernel** that allows the boundaries to curve. Two parameters control this,
and we will optimise both below:

* `sigma` controls how flexible (curved) the boundaries can be.
* `cost` controls how strictly the boundaries must separate the markers. A high
  cost penalises misclassified markers heavily, while a low cost tolerates some
  in exchange for simpler boundaries.

For each protein, the SVM also returns a **score** reflecting how far it lies
from a boundary: proteins deep within a compartment's region get high scores,
whereas proteins near a boundary get low scores. The score is a measure of
confidence, but it is not a probability.

::: {.callout-note}
#### The four steps of SVM classification in `pRoloc`

1. **Optimise** the SVM parameters `sigma` and `cost` using the markers
   (`svmOptimisation`)
2. **Check** the results of the optimisation (`getF1Scores`, `levelPlot`) and
   extract the best parameters (`getParams`)
3. **Classify** all proteins using these parameters (`svmClassification`)
4. **Threshold** the predictions so that only confident assignments are kept
   (`orgQuants`, `getPredictions`)
:::


### Optimising SVM parameters

As is the case with most supervised learning models, before we can perform any
classification the model parameters need to be optimised. We adopt a classical
view of training the model parameters and split the data into training and
testing sets. By default in `pRoloc` all methods allocate 80% of the labelled
data (marker proteins) for training and optimisation via cross-validation of the
free parameters, namely `sigma` and `cost`. The remaining 20% labelled data acts
as the test set to which the optimised parameters are applied in order to
calculate F1 scores. Briefly, an F1 score can be used as a measure of model
accuracy as it combines measurements of both precision and recall. A higher F1
score indicates a better quality classifier.

In `pRoloc` the SVM optimisation process is facilitated by the `svmOptimisation`
function. We pass our `MSnSet` object (here, `msn`) to the `svmOptimisation`
function and tell it the name of the `fData` column where our markers are held
(here `"markers"`). We use the `times` argument to specify how many iterations
of cross-validation to complete and the `xval` argument to set the value of *n*
in n-fold cross validation. Here, we will use the default 5-fold
cross-validation (`xval = 5`) with 10 iterations (`times = 10`). We would
typically set `times = 100`, but we use 10 here to keep the run time manageable;
100 iterations can take an hour or more on a laptop. Since our training data
contains asymmetric class sizes (subcellular compartments with variable numbers
of marker proteins), we also set class weights using the `class.weights`
argument to avoid biasing our localisation towards compartments with a greater
number of marker proteins [@YiMinHuang2005]. Hence, we weight each subcellular
compartment by the inverse of the number of marker proteins it has. Finally, to
ensure reproducibility of our results we set a seed using the `seed` argument.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
## Get the number of markers per class
marker_tbl <- table(getMarkers(msn, verbose = FALSE))

## Set class weights as inverse of class frequencies
weights <- 1 / marker_tbl[names(marker_tbl) != "unknown"]
weights
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

    Chromatin       Cytosol      Endosome            ER         Golgi 
  0.014492754   0.002732240   0.030303030   0.004329004   0.026315789 
     Lysosome Mitochondrion       Nucleus    Peroxisome            PM 
  0.029411765   0.002890173   0.002487562   0.058823529   0.012195122 
   Proteasome  Ribosome 40S  Ribosome 60S 
  0.035714286   0.071428571   0.031250000 
```


:::
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
## SVM parameter optimisation (using times = 10 for demonstration, usually 100)
svm_params <- svmOptimisation(object = msn,
                              fcol = "markers",
                              times = 10,
                              xval = 5,
                              class.weights = weights,
                              seed = 399)
```
:::




The output of this code is an object of class `GenRegRes`, a dedicated data
container used to store the results of machine learning optimisation (see
@Breckels2018 for more details). Printing it gives a short summary of the
optimisation.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
svm_params
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}


### Checking the optimisation results

#### Best parameters in each iteration with `getF1Scores`

To see which pair of parameters resulted in the highest F1 score in each
iteration we can use the `getF1Scores` function. This gives a matrix with one
row per iteration.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
## Best F1 score, and the parameters that gave it, in each iteration
getF1Scores(object = svm_params)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
             F1 sigma cost
 [1,] 0.8226757   0.1   16
 [2,] 0.8773922   0.1   16
 [3,] 0.8347168   0.1   16
 [4,] 0.8497589   0.1   16
 [5,] 0.8704653   0.1   16
 [6,] 0.8324702   0.1   16
 [7,] 0.8839693   0.1   16
 [8,] 0.8560528   0.1   16
 [9,] 0.8833327   0.1   16
[10,] 0.8611609   0.1   16
```


:::
:::




How do we interpret this output?

* **Each row is one iteration of cross-validation.** In each iteration, a
  different random 20% of the markers was held back as a test set, every
  combination of `sigma` and `cost` was tested, and the best-performing
  combination was recorded.
* **The best parameters are consistent across iterations.** Here,
  `sigma` = 0.1 and `cost` = 16
  give the highest F1 score in 10 of the 10 iterations.
  When the same combination wins in most or all iterations, the choice of
  parameters is stable and does not depend on how the markers happened to be
  split into training and test sets.
* **The F1 scores are high.** They range from 0.82 to
  0.88, with a mean of 0.86. The F1 score measures how well
  the model, trained on one part of the markers, predicts the markers it has
  not seen, balancing precision and recall. A score of 1 would be perfect, so
  our classifier correctly predicts most held-out markers. This is also a good
  sign that our curated markers separate the compartments well.
* **Some variation between iterations is expected.** The small spread in F1
  scores reflects which markers end up in each test set, and is not a cause
  for concern.

#### All parameter combinations with `levelPlot`

The `getF1Scores` function only tells us which combination of parameters
performed best in each iteration. It does not tell us how the other
combinations performed, or whether the best combination is clearly better than
its neighbours. For this, we can use the `levelPlot` function, which shows the
F1 score for every combination of `sigma` and `cost` tested during
optimisation as a heatmap.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
## Plot the average F1 score for every combination of sigma and cost
levelPlot(svm_params)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](P2_03_ml_classification_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){width=576}
:::
:::


Each cell of the heatmap is one combination of `sigma` and `cost`, and its
colour shows the F1 score for that combination averaged over the
iterations. When reading this plot, we look for three things:

* **Where the highest F1 scores are.** This shows us which region of parameter
  space gives the best classifier, and should agree with the results of
  `getF1Scores`.
* **Whether the best region is broad or narrow.** A broad region of similarly
  high F1 scores means the classifier is not very sensitive to the exact
  parameter values, which is reassuring. A single isolated cell with a high
  score is less trustworthy, as it may reflect chance.
* **Whether the best values lie at the edge of the grid.** If the highest F1
  scores are found at the smallest or largest value of `sigma` or `cost`
  tested, a value outside this range might perform even better. In that case,
  it is worth re-running `svmOptimisation` with a wider range of values,
  passed to its `sigma` and `cost` arguments.

By default, `levelPlot` summarises the F1 scores across iterations using the
mean. We can change this with the `fun` argument. For example, using the
standard deviation shows how much the performance of each combination varied
between iterations.

::: {.callout-exercise}
#### Challenge: How stable is the parameter search?
{{< level 1 >}}

Use `levelPlot` with `fun = median` and then `fun = sd`. Does the median give
the same best region as the mean? Which combinations of `sigma` and `cost`
give the most variable performance between iterations?

::: {.callout-answer collapse=true}


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
## Median F1 score across iterations
levelPlot(svm_params, fun = median)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](P2_03_ml_classification_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-8-1.png){width=672}
:::

```{.r .cell-code}
## Standard deviation of F1 scores across iterations
levelPlot(svm_params, fun = sd)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](P2_03_ml_classification_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-8-2.png){width=672}
:::
:::


The median should highlight the same best region as the mean, because the
same parameters performed best in most or all iterations. The standard
deviation plot shows which combinations performed inconsistently between
iterations. Ideally, the best combination should have both a high average F1
score and a low standard deviation.

:::
:::

::: {.callout-note}
#### Other functions for exploring the optimisation
`pRoloc` has further functions for exploring a `GenRegRes` object. For
example, `f1Count(svm_params, t = 0.8)` counts how many times each combination
of `sigma` and `cost` gave an F1 score above a threshold `t`, and the full F1
matrix for each iteration can be accessed with `svm_params@f1Matrices`. With
only 10 iterations these add little to `getF1Scores` and `levelPlot`, but
they become more informative when `svmOptimisation` is run with the
recommended 100 or more iterations.
:::

#### Extracting the best parameters with `getParams`

When one combination of `sigma` and `cost` performs best in most iterations,
the choice is clear. When several combinations perform similarly, the
`getParams` function chooses the *best* parameters for us. We use it here to
confirm the parameters that will be used for classification.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
## Return optimal parameters
getParams(object = svm_params)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
sigma  cost 
  0.1  16.0 
```


:::
:::


### Protein localisation prediction with SVMs

Now that we are happy with our parameters, we can apply the SVM model to our
data using the `svmClassification` function. Rather than typing the values of
`sigma` and `cost` by hand, we pass the whole `svm_params` object to the
`assessRes` argument, and the best parameters (those returned by `getParams`)
are extracted automatically. We again provide our weights to `class.weights`.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
## Carry out SVM classification using optimised parameters
msn <- svmClassification(object = msn,
                         fcol = "markers",
                         assessRes = svm_params,
                         class.weights = weights)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "markers"
```


:::
:::


After carrying out the SVM classification, we now have two new columns added to
the `fData` of our `MSnSet`.


::: {.cell}


### Thresholding protein localisation classification using an SVM

As we saw above, all proteins have been classified to one of the subcellular
compartments included in our training data. However, when applying a supervised
machine learning algorithm it is standard practice to set a specific confidence
threshold at which we accept new assignments. Any protein with a confidence below
this threshold will receive the final classification of `"unknown"`. The way in
which confidence is defined differs between classification algorithms. In the
case of SVMs, we rely on the SVM score to set our thresholds.

Let's plot a boxplot of the SVM scores of proteins allocated to each subcellular
compartment. We first use the `unknownMSnSet` function to return an `MSnSet` with
the marker proteins removed. Markers are assigned to their own class with a
score of 1, so they cannot tell us anything about the confidence of new
predictions.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
## Remove markers
msn_preds <- unknownMSnSet(object = msn)

## Use the same colours as plot2D for each compartment
org_cols <- getStockcol()[seq_along(getMarkerClasses(msn))]
names(org_cols) <- getMarkerClasses(msn)

## Visualise svm scores per organelle
msn_preds |>
  fData() |>
  as_tibble() |>
  ggplot(aes(x = svm, y = svm.scores, fill = svm)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7, outlier.size = 0.8) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = org_cols) +
  labs(x = "SVM classification", y = "SVM score") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
        legend.position = "none")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](P2_03_ml_classification_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-14-1.png){width=768}
:::
:::


We can see that each compartment displays a different distribution of SVM
scores and, therefore, applying a global score threshold would not be
appropriate here. Instead, there are several ways in which users can apply
compartment-specific thresholding. One common approach is to manually set a
compartment-specific FDR to allow up to 5% false discoveries, for example. This
would involve putting the proteins localised to each compartment in descending
order by their SVM score before going down the list to find the SVM score at
which 5% of proteins are incorrectly classified based on reliable subcellular
databases and prior knowledge from the literature. Unfortunately, such an
approach can never be completely objective and is limited to organisms with well
annotated subcellular proteomes. An alternative method would be to threshold
each compartment at a set percentile of its SVM scores. Here, we will
demonstrate the latter approach using the `orgQuants` and `getPredictions`
functions within `pRoloc`.

The `orgQuants` function takes an `MSnSet` containing classification results as
its input. We pass the column in our `fData` where the classification
assignments are stored (here `"svm"`), the score column (`"svm.scores"`) and the
marker column (`"markers"`). Finally, we use the `t` argument to specify our
threshold quantile. The quantile threshold is ultimately up to the user and will
depend on (1) how exploratory the analysis aims to be, and (2) the data quality
and resolution. In reality, we recommend testing multiple thresholds. Here, we
demonstrate the use of a 0.75 quantile threshold, which keeps the 25% of
proteins with the highest scores in each compartment.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
## Get organelle-specific quantile SVM scores
score_thresholds <- orgQuants(object = msn,
                              fcol = "svm",
                              scol = "svm.scores",
                              mcol = "markers",
                              t = 0.75)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

    0.9047257     0.9666035     0.7782578     0.8996244     0.8165128 
     Lysosome Mitochondrion       Nucleus    Peroxisome            PM 
    0.8149895     0.9865175     0.9559535     0.5448634     0.8227900 
   Proteasome  Ribosome 40S  Ribosome 60S 
    0.6746489     0.4903360     0.6929863 
```


:::
:::


We can now use these quantile-based score thresholds in the `getPredictions`
function.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
## Use organelle-specific quantiles to get thresholded localisation predictions
msn <- getPredictions(object = msn,
                      fcol = "svm",
                      scol = "svm.scores",
                      mcol = "markers",
                      t = score_thresholds)
```

::: {.callout-note}
#### Why would proteins not meet the classification threshold and remain unknown?

After thresholding our SVM classifications we have
5277 proteins which were not assigned to
one of the subcellular compartments and instead remain as `"unknown"`. There
are a number of reasons for which proteins may remain unknown after
classification. Firstly, the subcellular structure and compartmentalisation of a
cell is extremely complex and cannot be completely represented by our labelled
training data (markers). For instance, some subcellular structures may have too
few well-established marker proteins to be included in classification. This
could be due to lack of prior knowledge or absence of a unique protein profile,
as seen with P-bodies and stress granules, niches which are defined by many of
the same proteins. Secondly, a large proportion of the proteome is known to
reside in multiple subcellular niches within a given cell at a given time
[@Thul2017]. The abundance profiles of these multi-localised proteins can
represent a mixture of their localisations and, therefore, no longer match the
marker profiles of any given compartment. Further, since correlation profiling
experiments utilise bulk proteomics, the observed protein abundance profiles
represent an average of the population. Proteins which differ in subcellular
localisation across a heterogeneous starting population (e.g., due to
differences in cell cycle status) could also display mixed localisation
profiles and ultimately remain classified as `"unknown"`.
:::


## Classification using TAGM-MAP

As an alternative to protein localisation classification using a classical SVM
approach, users can also make use of newer Bayesian models available within
`pRoloc`. The main advantages of applying a Bayesian framework are that (1)
protein localisation predictions come with probabilities, which are on the same
scale for every compartment and are, in principle, easier to interpret than SVM
scores, and (2) the model includes an outlier component, so proteins that do
not fit any of the known compartments can be identified explicitly rather than
being forced into one. As we will see, however, these probabilities are only
as good as the model that produces them, and they need to be interpreted with
care.

Both Bayesian classifiers available within `pRoloc` are based on a t-augmented
Gaussian mixture (TAGM) model, as outlined in @Crook2018. In this course we use
the first implementation of this model, TAGM-MAP, which uses *maximum a
posteriori* estimates of the model parameters. The second implementation,
TAGM-MCMC, is not covered here (see @Crook2019 for a worked example). Unlike
TAGM-MCMC, TAGM-MAP does not sample the entire posterior distribution but
instead uses an extended version of the expectation maximisation (EM)
algorithm for inference. In terms of user experience, this means that TAGM-MAP
is faster and requires less computational power. However, it also means that
TAGM-MAP finds a single best set of model parameters and does not account for
uncertainty in them. We will return to the consequences of this when we
compare the SVM and TAGM-MAP results.

::: {.callout-note}
#### Bayesian methods, posteriors and the EM algorithm in brief

* **Bayesian methods** combine what we already believe (the **prior**) with
  what we observe in the data (the **likelihood**) to give an updated belief,
  the **posterior**. Here, the posterior tells us how probable it is that a
  protein belongs to each compartment, given its profile and the markers.
* **TAGM** (t-augmented Gaussian mixture) describes each compartment as a
  cloud of points with a centre and a spread (a Gaussian distribution), fitted
  to the markers. An extra, very broad component (a *t*-distribution) captures
  **outliers**: proteins that do not fit any compartment well.
* **MAP** (*maximum a posteriori*) means finding the single most probable set
  of model parameters, i.e. the best centre and spread for each compartment.
* The **EM algorithm** (expectation maximisation) is how TAGM-MAP finds these
  parameters. It alternates between two steps: (E) given the current
  compartment shapes, estimate how likely each protein is to belong to each
  compartment, and (M) given these estimates, update the compartment shapes.
  It repeats until the results stop changing, which is why we check
  **convergence**.
* **TAGM-MCMC** (Markov-chain Monte Carlo), which we do not cover here, does
  not stop at a single best set of parameters. Instead, it samples many
  plausible sets, which gives a fuller picture of uncertainty but takes much
  longer.
:::


### Optimising TAGM-MAP model parameters

The first step in using TAGM-MAP is executing the `tagmMapTrain` function. We
run the algorithm for 100 iterations (the default, `numIter = 100`). We set a
seed to ensure reproducibility and pass our marker annotated `MSnSet` to the
function.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
## Optimise the tagm-map model
set.seed(2)
map_params <- tagmMapTrain(msn, numIter = 100)
```
:::




The output of the `tagmMapTrain` function is an object of class `MAPParams`
which contains the optimised model parameters. Importantly, before applying
these parameters we need to check that the model has converged. The TAGM-MAP
expectation maximisation (EM) algorithm iterates between an expectation and
maximisation step until the log-posterior is stable. To check that the model
successfully reached this status, we use the `logPosteriors` function to extract
the log-posteriors at each iteration and pass this to the `plot` function.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
## Plot to visualise convergence
map_params |>
  logPosteriors() |>
  plot(type = "b", col = "blue", cex = 0.3,
       ylab = "log-posterior",
       xlab = "Iteration")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](P2_03_ml_classification_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-20-1.png){width=576}
:::
:::


We can see that the value of the log-posterior increased until it
stopped changing, thus indicating that the TAGM-MAP model has converged. This
means that it is suitable to continue with our optimised parameters. For further
details of the algorithm we refer readers to @Crook2019.


### Protein localisation prediction with TAGM-MAP

Next, we apply the optimised TAGM-MAP parameters to carry out protein localisation
classification via the `tagmMapPredict` function. We pass our `MSnSet` object and
the object storing our parameters, here called `map_params`.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
## Predict protein localisation using converged parameters
msn <- tagmMapPredict(object = msn, params = map_params)
```
:::


The `tagmMapPredict` function adds three new columns to the `fData` of our
`MSnSet`:

* **`tagm.map.allocation`**: the most probable compartment for each protein.
  Like the `svm` column, every protein is assigned to a compartment at this
  stage, before any thresholding.
* **`tagm.map.probability`**: the probability that the protein belongs to its
  allocated compartment, given the model. Values close to 1 indicate a
  confident allocation.
* **`tagm.map.outlier`**: the probability that the protein is an outlier,
  i.e. that it does not belong to any of the compartments defined by our
  markers. Values close to 1 indicate a protein that fits poorly with all
  compartments.

### Thresholding protein localisation classification using TAGM-MAP

As was the case when applying an SVM model, we still need to apply thresholding
to the initial classification results to ensure confidence in our results. Again,
proteins which do not meet our defined threshold will receive the final
classification of `"unknown"`. Thresholding of TAGM-MAP outputs can be achieved
by combining the probability of a predicted compartment classification being
correct with the probability that a protein belongs to an outlier component. In
the code chunk below we create a new column in the `fData` of our `MSnSet` called
`overall_prob`. This value is calculated as the probability of the compartment
classification multiplied by one minus the probability that a protein is an
outlier. Hence, a larger `overall_prob` indicates a higher confidence in our
classification.

Because these are probabilities, they are on the same scale for every
compartment, so we can use a single threshold for all compartments rather than
the organelle-specific thresholds we needed for the SVM. We use the
`getPredictions` function to update our classification predictions based on our
score column (`scol`) `overall_prob` with a threshold (`t`) of 0.999.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
## Store classification and outlier probabilities
tagm_prob <- fData(msn)[, "tagm.map.probability"]
tagm_out <- 1 - fData(msn)[, "tagm.map.outlier"]

## Create new column containing overall probability
fData(msn)[, "overall_prob"] <- tagm_prob * tagm_out

## Set prediction thresholds on overall probability
msn <- getPredictions(msn,
                      fcol = "tagm.map.allocation",
                      scol = "overall_prob",
                      t = .999)
```

The SVM scores are spread across the whole range from 0 to 1, so a threshold
can separate confident from less confident assignments. The TAGM-MAP
probabilities, by contrast, are almost all either very close to 0 or very
close to 1. With so few proteins in between, a threshold of 0.999 removes
very few proteins, and proteins lying between compartments are classified
with a probability of 1.

::: {.callout-note}
#### Why are the TAGM-MAP probabilities so extreme?

Probabilities are only as good as the model that produces them. There are
several reasons why TAGM-MAP tends to be overconfident:

* **TAGM-MAP finds a single best set of parameters.** It estimates the centre
  and spread of each compartment once, and treats these estimates as exact.
  It ignores any uncertainty in them, which makes the resulting probabilities
  more extreme than they should be. TAGM-MCMC (not covered here, see
  @Crook2019) averages over this uncertainty and generally produces more
  informative probabilities.
* **Many dimensions sharpen small differences.** Our data has 27
  quantitative channels (three concatenated replicates). With this many
  dimensions, a small difference in how well a protein fits two compartments
  becomes a very large difference in likelihood, pushing the probability
  towards 0 or 1.
* **Broad compartments absorb proteins between clusters.** A compartment
  with a large spread, such as the ER here, can fit proteins lying between
  clusters well enough to claim them with high probability.
* **The outlier component may be too small.** The expected proportion of
  outliers is set by a prior (see the `u` and `v` arguments in
  `?tagmMapTrain`). If our data contains more proteins that do not fit any
  compartment than the prior allows for, they are pushed into a compartment
  instead.
:::

### Which results should we use?

There is no single correct answer. Probabilities are attractive because they
are on the same scale for every compartment, are easy to interpret, and allow
us to identify outliers. However, as we have seen, the probabilities from
TAGM-MAP in this dataset are overconfident, and a fixed threshold
discriminates poorly between confident and uncertain assignments. There are
several ways to address this:

* use a stricter or organelle-specific threshold on the TAGM-MAP probabilities
  (see the challenge below)
* compare the predictions of different classifiers and focus on proteins on
  which they agree
* use TAGM-MCMC, which accounts for uncertainty in the model parameters and
  generally produces more informative probabilities, at a greater
  computational cost (see @Crook2019)

As with marker curation, the choice depends on the data and the question.
Whichever approach is used, predictions should always be checked against the
data, using spatial maps and protein profiles, and against prior knowledge.

**Task 4**

`orgQuants` works on any score, so the code runs without error. However, the
threshold means something different in each case:

* **SVM scores** are not probabilities and are not comparable between
  compartments, so setting a threshold relative to each compartment's own
  score distribution is a sensible way to choose cutoffs.
* **TAGM probabilities** are on the same scale for every compartment, so in
  principle a single threshold such as 0.999 should be enough. A quantile
  threshold ignores this: it keeps the top 25% of proteins in each
  compartment, regardless of their actual probability.

In practice, however, the TAGM-MAP probabilities in our data are very close to
0 or 1, so a fixed threshold of 0.999 removes very few proteins.
Organelle-specific quantiles bring back some discrimination within each
compartment and give results closer to those of the SVM. So, although
quantiles do not use the probabilities as probabilities, they can be a useful
practical tool when the probabilities are poorly spread. Whichever approach
you choose, check the results on a PCA plot and against prior knowledge.

::: {.callout-tip}
#### Key Points

* Supervised classifiers predict the localisation of unknown proteins by
  comparing their correlation profiles with those of the markers. Proteins can
  only be assigned to compartments represented in the marker list.
* SVM parameters (`sigma` and `cost`) are optimised by repeated
  cross-validation on the markers with `svmOptimisation`. Class weights stop
  the classifier favouring compartments with many markers.
* `getF1Scores` shows the best parameters in each iteration and `levelPlot`
  shows how every combination performed. Consistent best parameters and high
  F1 scores indicate a stable, well-performing classifier.
* `svmClassification` assigns every protein to a compartment, so predictions
  must be thresholded. SVM scores differ between compartments, so
  compartment-specific thresholds (`orgQuants`, `getPredictions`) are more
  appropriate than a single global threshold.
* TAGM-MAP gives a localisation probability and an outlier probability for
  each protein. Probabilities are on the same scale for every compartment and
  are easier to interpret than SVM scores, but they are only as reliable as
  the model behind them.
* In our data, TAGM-MAP probabilities are overconfident, so a fixed threshold
  assigns more proteins than the SVM, particularly in regions between
  compartments. Visualising predictions on spatial maps, comparing
  classifiers and choosing thresholds carefully all help to identify
  confident predictions.
* Proteins that remain `"unknown"` after thresholding are not necessarily a
  problem. They may belong to compartments not in the marker list, reside in
  more than one location, or vary in localisation across the cell
  population.
:::
